q: In a Fischer projection, how are the bonds at each chirality center (the cross) oriented in space?
c: Horizontal bonds point toward the viewer; vertical bonds point away
Vertical bonds point toward the viewer; horizontal bonds point away
All four bonds lie in the plane of the page
The left bond points toward the viewer and the right bond points away
h: Picture the carbon chain curling back away from you, like a bow tie at each center.
w: A Fischer projection draws the main chain vertically, curving back behind the page, so vertical bonds go away from the viewer and horizontal bonds come toward the viewer. That is why it may be rotated 180° in the plane but not 90°.
x: This is reversed; the carbon chain (vertical) recedes behind the page and the horizontal groups project out.
A tetrahedral carbon cannot have all four bonds in one plane; the cross is shorthand for a 3-D arrangement.
Both horizontal bonds point toward the viewer; neither horizontal bond goes back.

q: What is the configuration of the chirality center in this Fischer projection of 2-bromopropanoic acid?
c: R: Br → CO<sub>2</sub>H → CH<sub>3</sub> is counterclockwise, reversed because H is on a horizontal bond
S: Br → CO<sub>2</sub>H → CH<sub>3</sub> is counterclockwise, and the H position does not matter
S: CO<sub>2</sub>H → Br → CH<sub>3</sub> is clockwise, reversed because H is on a horizontal bond
R: CO<sub>2</sub>H → Br → CH<sub>3</sub> is clockwise, and the H position does not matter
h: Rank the groups, trace 1 → 2 → 3, then check whether H is on a vertical (away) or horizontal (toward you) bond.
w: Priorities: Br > CO2H > CH3 > H. On the page Br (right) → CO2H (top) → CH3 (bottom) runs counterclockwise. H is on a horizontal bond, pointing toward you, so the true sense is the reverse: R.
x: When H is on a horizontal bond it points toward the viewer, so the direction read on the page must be reversed.
Br (Z = 35) outranks the carbon of CO<sub>2</sub>H; atomic number of the attached atom comes first.
Br outranks CO<sub>2</sub>H, and the H on a horizontal bond requires reversing the direction; this choice makes both errors.

q: Give the configuration of this stereoisomer of 2-bromo-3-chlorobutane (C2 carries Br, C3 carries Cl).
h: Treat each cross separately. The other stereocenter is just a substituent: at C2 it is CH(Cl)CH<sub>3</sub>.
w: C2: Br > C3 (Cl, C, H) > CH3 > H. Br (right) → C3 (down) → CH3 (up) is clockwise on the page; H is horizontal, so reverse: S. C3: Cl > C2 (Br, C, H) > CH3 > H. Cl (left) → C2 (up) → CH3 (down) is clockwise; H is horizontal, so reverse: S. The compound is (2S,3S).
x: This is the enantiomer; both centers were read on the page without reversing for the horizontal H.
C2 was read without reversing for the horizontal H; only C3 was handled correctly.
C3 was read without reversing for the horizontal H; only C2 was handled correctly.

q: Which Fischer projection represents a meso compound?
h: A meso compound needs identical top and bottom halves and a horizontal mirror line through the middle of the projection.
w: In III (tartaric acid) the top and bottom halves are the same, and the two OH groups are on the same side, so a horizontal mirror line maps the top half onto the bottom. It has two chirality centers but is achiral: III is meso.
x: I has the same ends as III, but the OH groups are on opposite sides, so there is no internal mirror line; it is one enantiomer of chiral tartaric acid.
II has OH groups on the same side but different ends (CHO and CH<sub>2</sub>OH), so the halves are not equivalent and the compound is chiral.
IV has identical ends, but OH and Cl make the two centers different, so no internal mirror plane is possible.

q: What is the relationship between Fischer projections I and II?
h: Try rotating I by 180° in the plane of the page. Which operations are allowed for a Fischer projection?
w: Rotating I by 180° in the plane puts CH2OH on top and CHO on the bottom, and every horizontal group swaps sides, giving exactly II. A 180° in-plane rotation keeps horizontal bonds toward the viewer, so it is allowed: the two are identical (both are (2R,3R)-2,3,4-trihydroxybutanal, D-erythrose).
x: The OH groups appear on the left in II, but that is the result of the 180° turn, not reflection; both centers are R in both projections.
Diastereomers would differ at one center; assigning R/S shows both centers match.
Both are 2,3,4-trihydroxybutanal with the same connectivity; only the drawing orientation differs.

q: Fischer projection II was made by rotating I by 90° clockwise in the plane of the page. What is the relationship between I and II?
h: After the turn, which groups now sit on the vertical bonds, and which way do vertical bonds point?
w: A 90° turn moves the horizontal groups (toward the viewer) onto vertical bonds, which by convention point away, and vice versa. That reverses the center: I is R (OH > CHO > CH3), II reads as S. So I and II are enantiomers. Only 180° in-plane turns are allowed.
x: A rotation is harmless for a 3-D model, but a Fischer projection has a fixed meaning for vertical and horizontal bonds; a 90° turn breaks it.
With only one chirality center there are just two stereoisomers, which are mirror images, so diastereomers are impossible.
The connectivity (2-hydroxypropanal) is unchanged; only the configuration is inverted.

q: Which Fischer projection (OH-bearing carbon in the upper row) represents the compound drawn?
h: Assign R/S to the drawn compound first, then assign each Fischer projection and look for the match.
w: The drawing is (2R,3S)-3-chlorobutan-2-ol. In the Fischer projections, with H horizontal, read each center and reverse. IV: C2 (OH left) is R and C3 (Cl left) is S, so IV matches. I is (2R,3R), II is (2S,3R) (the enantiomer) and III is (2S,3S).
x: I is (2R,3R): the OH carbon matches, but the Cl carbon is inverted.
II is (2S,3R), the enantiomer of the drawn compound; both centers are inverted.
III is (2S,3S): the Cl carbon matches, but the OH carbon is inverted.

q: Assign C2 and C3 of this aldotetrose (D-threose).
h: At C2, the CHO carbon (O, O, H) outranks C3 (O, C, H). At C3, C2 (O, C, H) outranks CH<sub>2</sub>OH (O, H, H).
w: C2: OH > CHO > C3 > H. OH (left) → CHO (up) → C3 (down) is clockwise on the page; H is horizontal, so reverse: S. C3: OH > C2 > CH2OH > H. OH (right) → C2 (up) → CH2OH (down) is counterclockwise; reverse: R. D-Threose is (2S,3R).
x: This is L-threose, the enantiomer; both centers were read without reversing for the horizontal H.
C2 was read without reversing for its horizontal H; C3 is correct.
C3 was read without reversing for its horizontal H; C2 is correct.

h: Meso: two or more chirality centers and an internal mirror plane (so the molecule is achiral).
w: The 2,3-dibromobutane with opposite configurations (R and S) at two identically substituted centers has an internal mirror plane, so it is meso.
x: This is (2R,3R)-2,3-dibromobutane (or its mirror image); like-configured centers with identical substituents give a chiral compound.
The two centers carry different halogens (Br and Cl), so no internal mirror plane is possible; the compound is chiral.
This is a like-configured 2,4-pentanediol ((2R,4R) or (2S,4S)), which is chiral; only the (2R,4S) isomer is meso.

q: Which compound is a meso compound?
h: A meso compound must contain chirality centers and still be achiral. Check both requirements for each ring.
w: cis-1,2-Dichlorocyclopropane has two chirality centers (C1 and C2 each carry H, Cl, CH2 and CHCl) and a mirror plane through the CH2 carbon: it is meso.
x: trans-1,2-Dichlorocyclopropane has no mirror plane; it is chiral and exists as a pair of enantiomers.
cis-1,3-Dichlorocyclobutane is achiral, but it is not meso: C1 and C3 each have two identical ring paths, so the molecule has no chirality centers.
trans-1,2-Dichlorocyclobutane is chiral; only the cis-1,2 isomer has an internal mirror plane.

q: A pure compound has two chirality centers, is optically inactive, and cannot be resolved into enantiomers. It is best described as:
c: a conformational isomer of a chiral compound
h: Which kind of sample is optically inactive because of the molecule itself rather than a 50:50 mixture?
w: A meso compound has chirality centers but an internal mirror plane, so the molecule is superimposable on its mirror image: no rotation, and nothing to resolve.
x: A racemic mixture is also optically inactive, but it is a 50:50 mixture of enantiomers that can be resolved, not a single pure compound.
A pair of diastereomers is a mixture of two different compounds, not one pure compound, and each may rotate light.
Conformers of a chiral compound remain chiral and optically active.

q: How many stereoisomers exist for pentane-2,3,4-triol, CH<sub>3</sub>CH(OH)CH(OH)CH(OH)CH<sub>3</sub>?
h: Use symmetry. When C2 and C4 have the same configuration, is C3 still stereogenic? When they are opposite?
w: The molecule is symmetric end to end. If C2 and C4 match ((2R,4R) or (2S,4S)), the two halves at C3 are identical, so C3 is not stereogenic: one pair of enantiomers. If C2 and C4 are opposite ((2R,4S)), C3 becomes pseudoasymmetric and can be either of two forms, giving two different meso compounds. Total: 2 + 2 = 4.
x: 2<sup>3</sup> = 8 is only the maximum; symmetry makes several of those combinations the same molecule.
3 is the count for a two-center symmetric molecule such as 2,3-butanediol; here C3 adds a second meso form.
Six would require three pairs of enantiomers; the opposite-configured C2/C4 forms are meso, not pairs.

q: How many stereoisomers are possible for 2-bromo-3-chloropentane?
h: Count the chirality centers, then check whether any symmetry could reduce 2<sup>n</sup>.
w: C2 and C3 are both chirality centers, and the molecule has no symmetry that could create a meso form (the groups differ). So 22 = 4: two pairs of enantiomers.
x: 2 would be correct for a single chirality center; this molecule has two.
3 applies only when a meso form exists, which needs identically substituted centers.
8 would require three chirality centers.

q: How many stereoisomers are possible for 2,4-dibromopentane?
h: Two chirality centers, but look at the symmetry of the carbon chain.
w: C2 and C4 are chirality centers with identical substituent sets, and C3 is a CH2. (2R,4R) and (2S,4S) are enantiomers; (2R,4S) has an internal mirror plane through C3 and is meso. Total 3.
x: 2<sup>2</sup> = 4 counts (2R,4S) and (2S,4R) separately, but they are the same meso compound.
2 counts only the chiral pair and misses the meso isomer.
With only two chirality centers there cannot be more than four stereoisomers.

q: How many stereoisomers are possible for hex-4-en-2-ol, CH<sub>3</sub>CH(OH)CH<sub>2</sub>CH=CHCH<sub>3</sub>?
h: Look for every stereogenic unit, not just chirality centers.
w: There are two stereogenic units: the chirality center at C2 (R or S) and the C4=C5 double bond (E or Z). They are independent, so 2 × 2 = 4 stereoisomers: (2R,4E), (2S,4E), (2R,4Z), (2S,4Z).
x: 2 counts only the chirality center and ignores E/Z isomerism of the double bond.
No meso form is possible here, so nothing reduces the count below 2 × 2.
8 would require three stereogenic units; the molecule has only two.

q: This Fischer projection shows one stereoisomer of 3-chlorobutan-2-ol. How is it best described?
h: Erythro: the similar groups (here OH and Cl) on the same side of the Fischer projection. Then ask if a mirror line could exist when OH ≠ Cl.
w: OH and Cl are both on the right, so this is the erythro isomer. Because the two centers carry different groups (OH and Cl), there is no internal mirror plane: it is chiral ((2S,3R)). Erythro resembles meso in layout, but it is only meso when the two centers are identical.
x: Threo means the similar groups are on opposite sides; here OH and Cl are on the same side.
Erythro is a layout term; this molecule cannot be meso because OH and Cl make the halves different.
The groups are on the same side (erythro), and the molecule is chiral, not meso.

q: Which pair of stereoisomers of 3-bromobutan-2-ol is the threo pair?
h: Draw the Fischer projection with OH and Br on opposite sides, assign both centers, then find its mirror image.
w: Put CH3 top and bottom, OH on the right at C2 and Br on the left at C3 (threo, opposite sides). C2: OH > C3 > CH3; with H horizontal it reads S. C3: Br > C2 > CH3; it reads S. So threo = (2S,3S) and its enantiomer (2R,3R). The erythro pair is (2R,3S)/(2S,3R).
x: This is the erythro pair: in the Fischer projection, OH and Br are on the same side.
These two differ at only one center, so they are diastereomers (one threo, one erythro), not a pair.
These two differ at only one center, so they are one erythro and one threo isomer, not a pair of enantiomers.

q: The amino acid drawn is 2-amino-3-hydroxybutanoic acid. Which description fits it?
h: Assign R/S from the drawing, then build the Fischer projection (CO<sub>2</sub>H on top) and see whether NH<sub>2</sub> and OH fall on the same side.
w: C2: NH2 > CO2H > C3 > H gives S. C3: OH > C2 (N, C, H) > CH3 > H gives R. In the Fischer projection with CO2H up and CH3 down, NH2 is on the left at C2 and OH is on the right at C3: opposite sides, so threo, (2S,3R). This is natural L-threonine (its name, like the threo label, comes from threose).
x: In the Fischer projection NH<sub>2</sub> and OH fall on opposite sides, which is threo, not erythro.
C3 is R: OH > C2 (N, C, H) > CH<sub>3</sub>. (2S,3S) is allothreonine, a diastereomer.
(2S,3S) is allothreonine, which is erythro, but it is not the compound drawn; C3 here is R.
